title: Voices for a city guide app
scenario:
You run audio for a small company that makes narrated city walks. The team sent you four voice requests. Some want a real person's voice; one wants a new voice. You must decide what can go ahead, and how.

Use the exhibit. The company, the people and the requests are made up for this case. The rules and limits are from the vendors' pages in October 2026.
exhibit:
VOICE REQUESTS (made up)

  1. Gemini voice replication of Lena, a freelance narrator.
     Lena agreed by email. Plan: upload a 25-second clip of Lena
     reading, plus a consent clip where Lena says:
     "Hi, it's Lena, and I'm fine with you using my voice."

  2. ElevenLabs Professional Voice Clone of Lena, on the company
     account, made by Marco (the owner). Lena signed a consent form.

  3. The city's elected mayor is running for re-election. The campaign
     wants a campaign-style intro in a voice that sounds exactly
     like the mayor. The mayor said yes on the phone. Planned on ElevenLabs.

  4. A new narrator voice from ElevenLabs Voice Design.
     Description: "Warm male narrator, happy accent, studio reverb,
                   echo like a cathedral"
     Preview text: "STOP! Get out of here, right now!!!"

questions.prompt: Request 1 (Gemini): what must change before the replication can work?

options.text: Upload Lena's email as the consent file in place of the clip
options.explanation: Google asks for a consent recording: a real audio clip of the same speaker, not a document.

options.text: Have Lena read Google's exact consent statement in Lena's own voice
options.explanation: Right. Google's consent audio must be the same speaker clearly reciting the exact statement in a supported language.

options.text: Use a three-minute reference clip so the clone has more to learn
options.explanation: Google asks for a 10 to 30 second reference clip. The consent clip is the problem here.

options.text: Have Marco read the consent statement, since Marco owns the company
options.explanation: The Gemini API docs say the consent clip must be the same speaker as the reference audio: Lena, not Marco.

questions.prompt: Request 2 (ElevenLabs Professional Voice Clone): what is the right way forward?

options.text: Marco makes it on the company account and uploads Lena's form
options.explanation: The ElevenLabs docs say you can only make a Professional Voice Clone of your own voice, even with the other person's consent.

options.text: Marco makes it and passes the voice captcha with Lena's audio
options.explanation: ElevenLabs' policy forbids circumventing voice verification systems such as Voice CAPTCHA. It is still not Marco's voice.

options.text: Marco makes it on a free plan first, to test it before paying
options.explanation: The ElevenLabs docs say Professional Voice Clones need a Creator plan or above, and only of your own voice.

options.text: Lena makes and verifies it on Lena's account, then shares it privately
options.explanation: Right. The ElevenLabs docs say the voice owner creates and verifies the clone on their own account and can share it with a private link.

questions.prompt: Request 3: the mayor said yes to the campaign intro. What does ElevenLabs' Prohibited Use Policy say?

options.text: It is allowed if the mayor records a proper consent clip first
options.explanation: A consent clip from the mayor is not enough. The policy forbids political campaigning without ElevenLabs' prior written consent.

options.text: Not without ElevenLabs' written consent, even with the mayor's yes
options.explanation: Right. The policy's elections section forbids political campaigning without ElevenLabs' prior written consent. The mayor's yes is not that consent.

options.text: It is allowed if the clip is clearly labelled as made with AI
options.explanation: A label does not change this rule. The policy forbids political campaigning without ElevenLabs' prior written consent.

options.text: It is allowed with a designed voice that names the mayor
options.explanation: The tool does not matter: it is still political campaigning, which needs ElevenLabs' prior written consent. Naming the mayor aims to copy the mayor's voice.

questions.prompt: Request 4 (ElevenLabs Voice Design): which rewrite fits the vendor's guide best?

options.text: Keep reverb and echo, add "perfect audio quality", keep the text
options.explanation: The ElevenLabs docs say FX words like reverb and echo can hurt output quality, and the angry preview clashes with a warm voice.

options.text: Name the language and region first, drop FX words, use calm text
options.explanation: Right. The ElevenLabs docs say to name the language and variant first, avoid FX words, and use preview text that matches the voice.

options.text: Shorten it to one word, "narrator", and keep the angry preview
options.explanation: A short prompt can work, but the ElevenLabs docs say the preview text should match the voice. This one clashes.

options.text: Add a famous narrator's name so the model knows the exact sound
options.explanation: Naming a real person aims to copy their voice; the policy forbids synthesizing or impersonating a living person's voice without their explicit and informed consent or other valid authorization.
